Original Question: Every year, teams of competitive programmers from universities around the world compete in final of prestigious programming contest for title. In one particular year, I discovered that a team featuring an Australian coder won championship. This coder has impressive track record: secured bronze, silver, gold, and another silver medal in four consecutive IOIs. His other two teammates were from the same country. Could you tell me the year associated with the competition title and the name of the host university for the year he won that title?

We need identify what must be established to answer: year associated with competition title (the year he won championship), and host university name for that year. Need requirements.

Key entities:
- A prestigious programming contest, annual final, teams of competitive programmers from universities worldwide.
- In particular year, a team featuring an Australian coder won the championship.
- The coder's IOI medal sequence: bronze, silver, gold, another silver in four consecutive IOIs.
- His other two teammates were from the same country (as him? likely Australia? "His other two teammates were from the same country." Ambiguous same country as each other? The coder is Australian, so likely same country = Australia. But preserve: "from the same country" likely same country as the coder? We can state as in question: his other two teammates were from the same country. Preserve relation. Don't assume? We can keep "the same country" maybe same as the coder or same as each other? The text: "His other two teammates were from the same country." Could mean same country as him (Australia). We'll phrase exactly: "The other two teammates on the team were from the same country." But same country relative to? The original likely means same country as him? We can say "the same country as the Australian coder" if we infer? But rule preserve role identity uncertainty; country identity? "same country" refers to previously mentioned coder's country? It says "His other two teammates were from the same country." In context, the coder is Australian, so his teammates were from Australia. But to avoid outside inference, maybe phrase: "The other two teammates on the team were from the same country (as indicated in the question)." Hmm.

- Ask: year associated with competition title and host university for the year he won that title.

Need decompose into requirements:
1. Identify the annual prestigious programming contest final/title (object).
2. Identify the particular year in which a team featuring an Australian coder won the championship.
3. Identify the Australian coder on that team.
4. Verify that coder's IOI medal record: bronze, silver, gold, another silver in four consecutive IOIs. (This is condition for identifying coder maybe)
5. Verify the other two teammates were from the same country.
6. Determine the year associated with the competition title (the championship win year).
7. Determine the host university for that year (the year he won the title).

But requirements should be candidate requirements to be established. Could combine contest identification and title. Need not be atomic. Minimum that preserves semantic structure.

Let's consider what is asked: "Could you tell me the year associated with the competition title and the name of the host university for the year he won that title?" The final requested attributes: year, host university name. The year is associated with competition title. The host university for that year. So requirements:

R1: Identify the prestigious annual programming contest whose final involves university teams and whose championship title is at issue.
R2: Establish that in a particular year, a team that featured an Australian coder won that contest's championship.
R3: Identify that Australian coder (the one on the winning team) by his competitive programming track record: he won bronze, silver, gold, and another silver medal in four consecutive IOIs.
R4: Establish that the other two teammates on that winning team were from the same country (as each other? as the coder? The question says same country). We can phrase "the same country" without specifying? But it likely same country as the coder. Preserve exactly: "His other two teammates were from the same country." So requirement: "The other two teammates on the winning team were from the same country." But "same country" is a relation between the teammates? It could mean same country as the coder. Actually "same country" implies same as the coder? The sentence: "His other two teammates were from the same country." The pronoun "His" refers to coder; "same country" likely means same country as him. In English, "his other two teammates were from the same country" could mean they were from the same country as each other? Typically "same country" implies same country as the person mentioned? E.g., "John is Australian. His teammates were from the same country." = Australia. So we can say "the other two teammates were from the same country as the Australian coder." But rule 6 says preserve role identity uncertainty, not country identity. This is not role identity. We can interpret. But to be safe, maybe "the other two teammates were from the same country (as indicated by the question)." Hmm.

R5: Determine the year in which that championship was won (the year associated with the competition title).
R6: Determine the name of the host university for that year (the year of that championship win).

Could combine R5 and R6? The question asks both, but they are two requested attributes. Requirement 3 says candidate does not have to be logically atomic; keep complementary conditions together when they jointly identify or verify same object/event/relation. R5 and R6 are distinct attributes (year and host university) for same event (the competition in that year). Could be one requirement: "For the year in which the Australian coder's team won the championship, establish the year of that competition and the name of the host university for that year." But rule 4: Do not combine independent requirements merely because they contribute to same final answer. The year and host university are both final answers, but they are independent attributes. However they are about same event. The question asks "the year associated with the competition title and the name of the host university for the year he won that title." The year is the competition title year; host university is for that year. So they are linked: host university is for the year he won the title. So identifying the year is needed to identify host university. Could be separate: determine the year, then determine host university for that year. I think separate requirements are cleaner.

Also need identify the contest itself? The question doesn't name the contest, but describes it. To answer, we need know what contest. So requirement: "Identify the annual prestigious programming contest final described (teams of competitive programmers from universities around the world compete for a prestigious title)." That is necessary.

Also "championship" and "title" are same? The team won the championship. The question says "competition title" and "host university for the year he won that title." So title = championship.

Let's list candidate requirements:

- The contest is an annual final of a prestigious programming contest in which teams of competitive programmers from universities around the world compete for the prestigious title.
- In a particular year, a team featuring an Australian coder won the championship/title of that contest.
- The Australian coder on that team is identified by having won bronze, silver, gold, and another silver medal in four consecutive IOIs.
- The other two teammates on that winning team were from the same country (as the Australian coder?).
- The year associated with that championship/title is determined.
- The name of the host university for that year (the year of the championship win) is determined.

Maybe also "the coder's teammates were from the same country" is a condition to identify the team? The question says "His other two teammates were from the same country." This is part of the description of the team. It may be a condition to identify the winning team. So include.

Should we include "the team featured an Australian coder" and "his other two teammates were from the same country" as separate? They are complementary conditions about the team composition. Could combine into one requirement: "The winning team in the particular year featured an Australian coder and his other two teammates were from the same country." But rule 3 says keep complementary conditions together when they jointly identify same object/event/relation. They jointly identify the team. So maybe one requirement: "A team in a particular year won the championship; it featured an Australian coder and his other two teammates were from the same country." But the Australian coder's IOI record is separate to identify the coder. So:

R1: Identify the annual prestigious programming contest final described.
R2: Establish that in a particular year, a team won the championship of that contest, and that the team featured an Australian coder whose other two teammates were from the same country.
R3: Identify that Australian coder by his track record: bronze, silver, gold, and another silver medal in four consecutive IOIs.
R4: Determine the year of that championship win.
R5: Determine the host university for that year.

Could R2 and R3 be combined? R3 identifies the coder, R2 identifies the team. They are linked. But separate is fine.

What about "the year associated with the competition title" — is it the year he won the title? Yes. So R4.

Need ensure no outside knowledge. Don't mention IOI? The question says IOIs. So we can mention IOI. It's in source. That's fine.

Should we include "prestigious programming contest" as a requirement? It is a description of the contest. To answer, we need identify which contest. So yes.

Also rule 6: role identity uncertainty. We don't assume same/different. We refer to "the Australian coder" and "his other two teammates". That's fine.

Rule 7: temporal attachment. "four consecutive IOIs" attached to coder. "particular year" attached to win. "for that year" attached to host university. Good.

Rule 9: intermediate identification. We include identifying contest and coder.

Rule 11: no search queries etc. Our requirements are phrased as objectives, not queries. "Determine" is okay? It's a requirement. But maybe "Determine the year" is a requested attribute. That's fine. Avoid "search".

Should we include "the coder won the championship" as part of R2? Yes.

What about "the year associated with the competition title" — the title is the championship. So R5.

It might be that the year is the year of the competition final, and host university is the university that hosted the contest that year. So R6 is correct.
